title: The Twelve Networking Truths
summary: An April 1st humor RFC listing the fundamental truths of networking, such as things that cannot be fixed by more effort. It is satire.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1925 is an April 1st humor memo. It lists twelve 'fundamental truths' of networking, mixing real engineering lessons with jokes. The truths cover physical limits you cannot beat, the cost of complexity, and the value of simple designs. It is written in a straight-faced style but is not a technical standard.

questions: what are the twelve networking truths
what does rfc 1925 say about simplicity
subtitle: An April 1st memo that lists twelve half-serious truths about network design.

tldr.problem: Network engineers keep meeting constraints that effort cannot remove and design choices that have no perfect answer.
tldr.mechanism: The memo collects twelve fundamental truths, from physical limits such as the speed of light to design wisdom such as preferring to remove rather than add.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st joke document published as an Informational memo; it does not specify a standard, though it claims every standard implicitly follows these truths.

today: RFC 1925 is an Informational memo and an April 1st joke; it is not a technical standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Memo Is
sections.content:
RFC 1925 is an April 1st humor document. It claims to document the fundamental truths of networking, gathered, the editor says, from extensive study by many people, some of whom did not intend to contribute. The truths are meant to apply to networking in general, not only to TCP/IP or the Internet. The memo states that it does not specify a standard, except in the joking sense that all standards must implicitly follow these truths.

The first two truths set the tone. Truth 1 is simply "It Has To Work." Truth 2 says that no matter how hard you push and whatever priority you give it, you cannot increase the speed of light; its corollary notes that you cannot make a baby in much less than nine months, and that trying to speed this up might make it slower but will not make it happen quicker.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a joke RFC released on 1 April. Its first rule is that the network has to work. Its second is that effort cannot beat physics, such as the fixed speed of light.

sections.title: Truths About Complexity and Trade-offs
sections.content:
Several truths describe the cost and lure of complexity. Truth 3 observes that with sufficient thrust, pigs fly just fine, but that this is not necessarily a good idea, since it is hard to be sure where they will land. Truth 5 says it is always possible to glue multiple separate problems into a single complex interdependent solution, and that in most cases this is a bad idea. Truth 6 says it is easier to move a problem around, for example to another part of the architecture, than to solve it, with the corollary that it is always possible to add another level of indirection.

Truth 4 says some things in networking can never be fully understood by someone who has neither built commercial networking equipment nor run an operational network. Truth 7 says "It is always something," with the corollary that of good, fast and cheap you may pick any two. Truth 8 says it is more complicated than you think. Truth 11 warns that every old idea will be proposed again with a different name and presentation, whether or not it works, and its corollary points back to the rule about adding indirection.
sections.plainLanguage: These truths say you can always complicate a design or move a problem elsewhere instead of solving it, that some knowledge only comes from operating real networks, and that old ideas keep returning under new names.

sections.title: Truths About Resources and Perfection
sections.content:
Truth 9 says that for all resources, whatever it is, you need more, with the corollary that every networking problem takes longer to solve than it seems it should. Truth 10 says one size never fits all. Truth 12, the last and most directly about design, says that in protocol design perfection has been reached not when there is nothing left to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.

The memo's Security Considerations section says the RFC raises no security issues, while noting that security protocols are subject to the fundamental networking truths. Its References section says the references have been deleted to protect the guilty and avoid enriching the lawyers.
sections.plainLanguage: The last truths say you always need more resources, no single design suits everyone, and the best design is the one you can simplify the most.
